title: Fame forgets
hook: everyone who remembers you will soon die too (Meditations 4.19)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was time gained. Your line was run straight along the line, without swerving.
screen: `RUN STRAIGHT ALONG THE LINE, WITHOUT SWERVING.`

segments.voice: Name your great-grandparents. All eight of them, without looking anything up. These were people who worked, loved, worried about money, told jokes at dinner, and were, for a while, the center of somebody's world. Three generations on, some of their names have slipped even from their own family. Marcus Aurelius, whose face was stamped on coins across an empire, did that same arithmetic about himself, and used it to loosen the grip of wanting to be remembered. Today: fame forgets.
screen: `NAME ALL EIGHT GREAT-GRANDPARENTS.` → `THREE GENERATIONS LATER.` → `FAME FORGETS.`

segments.voice: In the nineteenth entry of book four Marcus writes about the person who longs to be remembered after death. They don't stop to think, he says, that every one of those who remember them will soon die too, and then those who come after, until the whole memory goes out, passed from one person to the next, through people who admire and then die. Then he pushes further. Suppose the people who remember you were immortal, and the memory too. What would that be to you? You'd be gone. Praise can't reach the dead. And to the living, he asks, what is praise, except for some practical use? Information, at best. It doesn't make the act better or worse. So what's left is the act itself. Do good to be remembered, and you're building on something that will dissolve. Do it because it's good, and it's complete the moment it's done. This can sound bleak. But look at the questions it answers: will anyone notice, will this count, will they know it was me? Marcus sets them down. In the end, nobody will remember. So the good thing can be done without an audience, the way a great-grandmother might once have fed a neighbor's child and never written it down. Her name may be gone. The meal was still eaten.
screen: `EVERYONE WHO REMEMBERS WILL DIE TOO.` · `EVEN IF THEY DIDN'T, WHAT IS IT TO YOU?` · `PRAISE DOESN'T CHANGE THE ACT.` · `THE ACT IS COMPLETE WHEN DONE.` · then, large: `NO CREDIT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone in your family line whose name you don't know, two or three generations back, and picture them at the end of an ordinary day, having done some small good nobody wrote down. Let them be uncredited, and complete. Then think of one good you could do for no credit, something nobody will know was you.
Fame forgets. Marcus notes that everyone who remembers you will die too; so do good for its own sake, complete without credit. Today's word.
Your line: no credit. Done well, and done, is enough, credited or not. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes answer Meditations 4.19 with anonymous acts: a good deed done so that no one will know who did it.

original.note: Greek, 'after-fame', fame after death: the craving Marcus answers in 4.19. The same word ends book two: after-fame is oblivion.

notes: 4.19 paraphrased: he who has a vehement desire for posthumous fame does not consider that every one who remembers him will himself also die very soon, then those who succeed them, until the whole remembrance is extinguished as it is transmitted through men who foolishly admire and perish; suppose those who remember were immortal, what is it to you? And to the living, what is praise, except for some utility? Confirm.
The Greek for posthumous fame in 4.19 is often given as husterophemia; the trapdoor paraphrases it as 'after-fame'. Confirm. The original game uses the common word doxa.
Marcus's portrait on coinage across the empire: standard; confirm wording.
